title: Treasury Laws Amendment (Combating Multinational Tax Avoidance) Bill 2017
short_title: Treasury Laws Amendment (Combating Multinational Tax Avoidance) Bill 2017

speeches.speaker: Andrew Leigh
speeches.brief: The government's bill hides a $50 billion tax cut for big banks and multinationals behind a weak approach to multinational tax avoidance, raising only $200 million. Labor supports the bill but calls for an explanation, and notes its own proposals would raise $1.6 billion over the forward estimates.

speeches.speaker: Ted O'Brien
speeches.brief: The speaker argued that the coalition government has already clawed back $2 billion in multinational tax avoidance this financial year and that the Treasury Laws Amendment (Combating Multinational Tax Avoidance) Bill will strengthen Australia's global leadership in addressing the problem.

speeches.speaker: Matt Thistlethwaite
speeches.brief: The speaker argued the government's bill is a "soft touch" that raises only $200 million, whereas Labor's stronger reforms would have raised $1.6 billion over forward estimates and $5.9 billion over a decade. They criticized the government for proposing a $50 billion tax cut for big businesses and banks while cutting services for pensioners, the disabled, and low-income Australians.

speeches.speaker: Kevin Hogan
speeches.brief: The speaker argued for the Treasury Laws Amendment (Combating Multinational Tax Avoidance) Bill 2017 and the Diverted Profits Tax Bill 2017, which impose a 40% penalty rate on diverted profits and increase penalties for large multinationals (e.g., up to $525,000 for late lodgement). The laws are expected to claw back $2 billion in tax this financial year, raise $200 million over forward estimates, and have already prompted Facebook and Google to restructure their Australian tax arrangements.

speeches.speaker: Trevor Evans
speeches.brief: The speaker argued in favour of the Treasury Laws Amendment (Combating Multinational Tax Avoidance) Bill 2017, stating the government has already recovered $2 billion from multinationals and expects the bill to raise $100 million annually from 2018-19. The bill increases maximum administrative penalties for significant global entities from about $5,000 to over $500,000 and introduces a 40% penalty rate on diverted profits, effective 1 July 2017.

speeches.speaker: Matt Keogh
speeches.brief: Labor supported the Treasury Laws Amendment (Combating Multinational Tax Avoidance) Bill 2017, but argued the government’s approach raised only $200 million compared to Labor’s proposed $1.6 billion, while net debt had blown out from $184 billion to $317 billion under the Liberals and 109 large companies paid no tax. The speaker criticised the government for cutting 3,000 ATO jobs, giving a $50 billion tax cut mainly benefiting foreign shareholders, and failing to properly fund Medicare, schools, and family payments.

speeches.speaker: Julie Owens
speeches.brief: The government's multinational tax avoidance bill will raise only $200 million over the forward estimates, compared to Labor’s proposed $1.6 billion, while the government cut 3,000 ATO staff and gave $50 billion in business tax cuts.

speeches.speaker: Wayne Swan
speeches.brief: The Treasury Laws Amendment (Combating Multinational Tax Avoidance) Bill 2017 raises only $200 million, far below the estimated $13 billion in lost tax revenue, and fails to address debt deduction loopholes; BHP and Rio Tinto were named for transfer pricing and tax evasion, while the $50 billion corporate tax cut was opposed as ineffective trickle-down economics.

speeches.speaker: Rebekha Sharkie
speeches.brief: The speaker supported the Treasury Laws Amendment (Combating Multinational Tax Avoidance) Bill 2017 but urged the government to strengthen it by reducing the threshold for "significant global entities" from $1 billion to $250 million, lowering the "sufficient foreign tax" test from 20% to 10%, and requiring multinationals to disclose potential diverted profit tax liabilities with penalties for non-disclosure. The speaker cited Apple shifting $8.9 billion in unpaid taxes to Ireland, Google paying $16 million in tax on $2.5 billion in estimated revenue, and Facebook Australia paying $814,000 in tax on an estimated $500–600 million in advertising revenue.
